Heritage sites by state

Heritage sites in Manipur: Kangla, Loktak and living traditions

Manipur's heritage centres on Kangla, the old seat of the Meitei kings in Imphal, along with the Shree Govindajee temple, the women's market of Ima Keithel, Moirang and Loktak Lake, the Khongjom war memorial, the prehistoric Khangkhui cave and the living arts of Manipuri dance and Thang-Ta. The state has no UNESCO World Heritage Site.

We offer lectures on Manipur's history and living traditions online, and plan study tours on request when travel conditions allow.

Why Manipur's heritage matters

Manipur is a valley ringed by hills, between the Brahmaputra plains and Myanmar. The Meitei kingdom in the valley kept a royal chronicle, the Cheitharol Kumbaba, which records reigns traditionally from the 1st century CE, though historians treat the earliest entries with caution. The hills are home to Naga and Kuki-Zo communities, among others, with their own histories, villages and traditions.

Manipur's history includes the adoption of Vaishnavism at the court in the 18th century, wars with Burma, including the period of Burmese occupation from 1819 to 1826 known as the Chahi Taret Khuntakpa (Seven Years' Devastation), the Anglo-Manipur war of 1891, and the Battle of Imphal in 1944 during the Second World War. For background on the hill communities, see our tribes of India guide.

Kangla: the heart of Manipur

Kangla, in the centre of Imphal on the Imphal river, was the seat of Meitei kings for many centuries and the political and religious centre of the kingdom. It holds sacred sites of the indigenous Sanamahi religion, the remains of the Govindajee temple of the royal period, a coronation hall area, moats and the large Kangla Sha (dragon-lion) figures, which were rebuilt in recent decades after the British destroyed the originals in 1891.

After the 1891 war the British used Kangla as a base, and later it was occupied by Indian security forces. It was handed back to the state government in 2004 and is now a protected heritage site. Its story shows how a place can carry royal, religious, colonial and modern political meanings at once, a theme in our session on who owns the past.

Temples, markets and memorials in Imphal

The Shree Govindajee temple, next to the later royal palace, is the main Vaishnava temple of Manipur, with twin domes and a large hall for ritual dance. Manipuri Ras Lila performances, central to Manipuri classical dance, are held at temples like this. The Sanamahi temples and shrines of the Lai Haraoba festival honour indigenous deities.

Ima Keithel, the Mothers' Market, is run entirely by women traders and has a history of several centuries; women of Manipur have led important protests, including the Nupi Lan (Women's War) of 1904 and 1939, a history marked by a memorial in Imphal. The Imphal and Maibam Lokpa Ching war cemeteries and memorials recall the 1944 battles. Our talk on cemeteries, epitaphs and public memory gives groups a way to read such places.

Archaeological sites and natural heritage

Khangkhui cave, in Ukhrul district, is a limestone cave where excavations yielded stone tools and animal bones, and is usually placed in the Palaeolithic. Other cave and rock shelter sites have been reported in the hills, though excavation in Manipur remains limited and dates are often broad. Our Stone Age in India guide sets the context.

Loktak Lake, near Moirang, is the largest freshwater lake in the north-east and is known for its floating islands of vegetation (phumdis). Keibul Lamjao National Park, on the lake, is the only floating national park in the world and the home of the sangai deer. Moirang is linked to the Khamba-Thoibi epic and was where the Indian National Army raised its flag in 1944. Khongjom, in Thoubal district, marks the last major battle of the 1891 war, remembered on Khongjom Day each April.

Living heritage: dance, martial arts and crafts

Manipuri dance, one of India's recognised classical dance forms, grew out of temple ritual and Ras Lila. Thang-Ta, the martial art of sword and spear, and Sarit Sarak, unarmed combat, are taught in traditional schools; our lecture on martial arts and society explores how such traditions carry history. Sagol Kangjei, a form of polo played on Manipuri ponies, is often described as one of the ancestors of modern polo. Longpi black pottery from Ukhrul, made without a wheel, is a notable craft.

Sources for Manipur's history

Manipur's past is known from an unusual mix of sources. The Meitei language has its own script, Meitei Mayek, which was used for chronicles, genealogies and ritual texts (puya) before being replaced by Bengali script in the 18th century; it was revived in the late 20th century and is now taught in schools. Puyas, royal chronicles and court records give a Meitei view of events, while Burmese and British accounts give outside views of the wars of the 19th century.

Oral tradition carries much of the history of the hill communities, including migration stories, village founding and clan histories. Researchers increasingly combine oral history with archaeology and documents, and our oral history and neighbourhood memory lab teaches groups the basic methods. Archaeology in Manipur is still limited, so new survey and excavation could change the picture considerably.

The Lai Haraoba festival, held for the umang lai (forest and local deities), re-enacts the creation of the world, the building of houses and the planting of crops through dance and song. It is one of the clearest windows into the pre-Vaishnava religion of the Meitei and is studied by anthropologists and historians alike.

Planning a heritage visit to Manipur

Imphal is the base for Kangla, the Govindajee temple, Ima Keithel and the museums; Moirang and Loktak make a day trip. Ukhrul needs a longer journey. Indian visitors from outside the state need an Inner Line Permit, and the security situation can change, so check official advisories before planning. We can plan a study tour for your group or private journeys when conditions allow, and lectures online at any time.

Questions people ask

What are the main historical places in Manipur?

Kangla Fort, the Shree Govindajee temple, Ima Keithel, the Nupi Lan memorial and war cemeteries in Imphal; Moirang and Loktak Lake; Khongjom; the Bishnupur temple; and Khangkhui cave in Ukhrul are the main ones.

What is Kangla Fort?

Kangla, in central Imphal, was the seat of the Meitei kings for centuries and holds sacred sites of the Sanamahi religion. The British occupied it after 1891, and it returned to state control in 2004 as a heritage site.

Does Manipur have a UNESCO World Heritage Site?

No. As of October 2026 Manipur has no inscribed World Heritage Site. Keibul Lamjao National Park on Loktak Lake, the only floating national park in the world, is its best known natural heritage area.

Can Talaash Heritage arrange a Manipur heritage programme?

We can plan a custom study tour or private journey when travel conditions allow, and give online lectures on north-east history, martial arts and society, or heritage and memory at any time for schools and colleges.
